options: A BASE CASE, and a recursive case that moves TOWARDS it
explanation: Factorial: n <= 1 answers directly; n * Factorial(n-1) shrinks n. Miss either and the stack overflows.

options: On the way BACK UP as calls return - the unwinding
explanation: Calls descend to the base case first; each frame then completes its pending multiply as results bubble back.

options: It CANNOT BE CAUGHT - the process dies; prevention is the only cure
explanation: Each call takes a frame (~1MB total budget). No base case, or too-deep descent on big input, and it is over - convert to a loop with an explicit Stack<T>.

stem: Fib(n) => Fib(n-1) + Fib(n-2) naively is O(2 to the n) because:
options: The SAME values are recomputed endlessly - Fib(20) takes 21,891 calls
explanation: Each call spawns two; the tree of repeated work doubles per level. The lesson counts the calls live.

stem: Adding a Dictionary cache to Fib changes its complexity to:
options: O(n) - each value computed exactly ONCE, then looked up
explanation: Fib(50): 49 computed entries, instant answer. Time bought with memory - 5.1's trade, powered by 3.2's dictionary.

stem: Anything recursive can be written iteratively, so recursion is chosen when:
options: It makes the code CLEARER - especially on recursive DATA like trees and folders
explanation: TotalSize(folder) in one line vs a loop juggling an explicit stack. For flat accumulation (factorial), the loop is arguably clearer.

stem: folder.Files.Sum(...) + folder.Folders.Sum(TotalSize) traverses any depth because:
options: The DATA is recursive - folders contain folders - so recursive code fits it exactly
explanation: The same shape powers trees (5.7), graphs (5.8), JSON, and merge sort's divide-and-conquer.

stem: Gcd(a, b) => b == 0 ? a : Gcd(b, a % b); What is Gcd(48, 18)?
explanation: 48,18 -> 18,12 -> 12,6 -> 6,0 -> 6. Two thousand years old, three tokens of C#.

stem: Towers of Hanoi with n discs needs how many moves?
options: 2 to the n minus 1 - 64 discs would outlast the universe
explanation: Move n-1 away, move the big disc, move n-1 back: M(n) = 2M(n-1) + 1. Legitimately exponential - no algorithm can beat it.

stem: Recursive binary search on a BILLION items overflows the stack: true or false, and why?
options: FALSE - depth is only ~30, because the range HALVES each call
explanation: Depth = log2(n), not n. Divide-and-conquer recursion is shallow; linear recursion (one item per call) is what overflows.
